## The problem

A single unit receives an intervention and we want its effect, but the
outcome of interest (the **target domain**) is only observed *after* the
intervention: there is no pre-intervention period to build a synthetic
control from. What we do have is a related **reference domain** observed for
the same units and untouched by the intervention (in the paper's
application: vaccination rates of a different subpopulation of the same
cities). `causalpanelfusion` fuses the two domains.

The inputs are four matrices with one row per unit:

| argument    | paper | content                                    |
|-------------|-------|--------------------------------------------|
| `target`    | $Y$   | target-domain outcomes (units × periods)    |
| `reference` | $F$   | reference-domain outcomes (units × periods) |
| `X`         | $X$   | target-domain covariates                    |
| `Z`         | $Z$   | reference-domain covariates                 |

We simulate data from the factor model used in the paper's simulation study
(with a smaller budget grid below to keep the vignette fast).

```{r}
library(causalpanelfusion)
sim <- simulate_fusion_data(n_units = 21, seed = 45)
dim(sim$target)
dim(sim$reference)
sim$psi   # true average effect on the treated unit
```

## Synthetic control data fusion

`scfusion()` learns donor weights in the reference domain with the paper's
data-driven constrained optimisation: covariate balance in both domains is
kept within a slack `eta_Z`, `eta_X` of the best attainable balance, and the
budget $b = (b_F, b_Z, b_X)$ trading off the three fit criteria is selected
from a grid. The weights are then transported to the target domain.

```{r}
fit <- scfusion(sim$target, sim$reference, X = sim$X, Z = sim$Z,
                budget_step = 0.05)
fit
```

`summary()` adds per-period effects, the selected budget, the fit criteria
and a covariate-balance table.

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

```{r}
plot(fit)                       # target domain
plot(fit, type = "reference")   # reference domain (where weights are fit)
```

The default grid (`budget_step = 0.01`, 4,796 candidates) matches the paper.
The optimisation uses the free ECOS solver; `solver = "gurobi"` reproduces
the original implementation if you have a Gurobi licence.

## Prediction intervals

`scfusion_pi()` decomposes the error into the weight-construction error
(bootstrap refits of the whole algorithm in the reference domain) and the
transfer error (calibrated from donor placebos in the target domain), and
reports Approach 2 (location-scale, Gaussian and empirical) and Approach 1
(sub-Gaussian) intervals at level `1 - alpha1 - alpha2`.

```{r}
pi <- scfusion_pi(fit, B = 100, seed = 1, progress = FALSE)
pi
```

Use `B = 500` (the default) for reported results. Each refit repeats the
budget search, so this is the slow step; run the refits in parallel with

```{r, eval = FALSE}
future::plan(future::multisession)
pi <- scfusion_pi(fit, parallel = TRUE, seed = 1)
```

The results are identical to the serial run. `budget_step = 0.05` (refits
only) or `reselect_budget = FALSE` give faster approximations.

Pointwise per-period bands:

```{r}
bands <- pi_bands(pi, method = "gaussian")
bands[, c("period", "treated", "synthetic", "total_lo", "total_hi",
          "effect", "effect_lo", "effect_hi")]
plot(pi)                      # bands on the synthetic control
plot(pi, type = "effect")     # per-period effects
```

Because the transfer error is not identified nonparametrically,
`sensitivity_pi()` traces the interval as its scale is multiplied by
$\rho$:

```{r}
sens <- sensitivity_pi(pi)
sens
plot(sens)
```

## Diagnostics

In-space placebos re-run the algorithm with every donor as a pseudo-treated
unit; the RMSPE-ratio test turns them into an exact placebo p-value, using
the reference-domain fit as the "pre-period".

```{r}
pl <- placebo_test(fit, progress = FALSE)
plot(pl)
rmspe_test(fit, progress = FALSE)
```

The leave-one-out check drops each positive-weight donor in turn:

```{r}
loo <- placebo_test(fit, type = "leave_one_out", progress = FALSE)
loo
```

Sensitivity of the estimate to the balance slack:

```{r}
es <- eta_sensitivity(fit, eta_Z = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2), eta_X = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2),
                      progress = FALSE)
es[, c("eta_Z", "eta_X", "estimate", "NSE_F", "n_donors")]
plot(es)
```

## Equi-confounding data fusion

The paper's second method anchors the target-domain confounding bias at the
reference-domain bias, either additively (linear) or multiplicatively
(logarithmic):

```{r}
ec <- equi_confounding(sim$target, sim$reference)
ec
plot(ec)
```

## Using your own data

Long-format panels are converted with `panel_to_matrix()` and covariates
with `covariate_matrix()`. Rows are matched by unit name, so the treated
unit can be given by name. For example, with one file of monthly outcomes
(columns `unit`, `group`, `month`, `rate`) and one file of covariates:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
outcomes <- read.csv("monthly_outcomes.csv")
covs <- read.csv("covariates.csv")

ref <- subset(outcomes, group == "reference")
tgt <- subset(outcomes, group == "target")
Fm <- panel_to_matrix(ref, unit = "unit", time = "month", outcome = "rate")
Y  <- panel_to_matrix(tgt, unit = "unit", time = "month", outcome = "rate")
vars <- c("median_income", "median_age", "proportion")
Z <- covariate_matrix(subset(covs, group == "reference"), "unit", vars,
                      normalize = TRUE)
X <- covariate_matrix(subset(covs, group == "target"), "unit", vars,
                      normalize = TRUE)

fit <- scfusion(Y, Fm, X = X, Z = Z, treated = "Chelsea")
```

## Reference

Yang, Z., Lee, S. H., Köhler, J. R. and Ghassami, A. Causal data fusion for
panel data without a pre-intervention period. arXiv:2410.16391.
